title: Tiered SLO kickoff notes + open questions (Hosted vs Dedicated)
content:
Date/time: 2026-01-15 (kickoff)
Facilitator: Sean Gallagher (SRE Director)
Notes owner: Rafael Mendes

Attendees (partial): Sean Gallagher, Rafael Mendes, Aisha Bello, Priya Natarajan, Ethan Park, Mina Haddad, Ravi Menon, Jordan Lee, Amara Diallo, Logan Wright, Nadia Rahman, Sergio Costa, Lauren Bishop, Marissa Cole, Paula Mendes, Cole Summers, Thomas Baird, Miles Thornton

Why we’re here (Sean):
- We have reliability expectations scattered across docs, tribal knowledge, and customer emails. We need one source of truth per product tier.
- We have alerts and incidents, but we don’t have a consistent “how close are we to unacceptable” signal that affects day-to-day release behavior.
- Goal of this program is not just a Confluence page. Goal is: the org feels error budget burn through gated releases + progressive rollouts + auto-mitigation.

Scope reminder (Rafael):
- In scope: Hosted API + Dedicated capacity. Tiered SLO tables, SLIs + calculations, dashboards, burn-rate alerting, enforcement/gates, routing degradation rules, incident/pager playbooks, comms triggers.
- Partial scope: Private (mapping guidance, optional targets, no hard gates initially).
- Out of scope: commercial SLA contract changes.

Current pain points (round robin; condensed):
1) Streaming is our #1 “but the customer says it was down” category
- Support sees “disconnects” as downtime; engineering often treats it as client abort.
- No single definition for streaming success. Some places count “sent 1 token” as success; others require full stream completion.
- Latency for streaming is ambiguous: TTFT vs end-to-end stream duration.

2) Tier expectations aren’t explicit; Dedicated customers assume stricter behavior
- Dedicated is sold as predictable throughput/isolation. Customers interpret that as “more reliable than Hosted,” but we don’t have measurable tier-specific targets and dashboards we can point to.
- Current internal dashboards are per-service and per-region; not aligned to customer journeys (chat/completions, embeddings) and not consistently filterable by tier.

3) Per-model variance + model churn
- Hosted model catalog changes weekly; performance profiles differ by model and quantization.
- Some incidents were “one model variant in one region,” but our global rollups hide it.
- Too much cardinality risk if we go fully per-model/per-route/per-region everywhere.

4) Enforcement is missing
- Today: “incident happens → postmortem → hopefully we learn.”
- Desired: “budget is burning → releases automatically constrained, rollouts slowed, mitigations kick in.”
- Need to avoid blocking urgent fixes; start with warn-only gates.

Principles (agreed at kickoff; may refine):
- Tier-aware targets: Dedicated generally stricter than Hosted, but must reflect real operational differences (isolation, capacity commitments, readiness).
- SLOs are about user journeys (API requests, streaming behavior, embeddings) more than internal components.
- SLIs must be consistent across regions and instrumented at the edge (gateway) with routing/runtime attribution as needed.
- All SLOs must explicitly list exclusions (invalid auth, rate-limit rejections, malformed requests, customer-side timeouts, etc.).
- We will have (a) “global tier dashboards” and (b) scoped views (region/model/route) for debugging and action.
- Error budget policy must change behavior (gates/approvals/rollout constraints), not just create alerts.

Initial SLO strawman (NOT final; used to start discussion)
Measurement window proposal: 28-day rolling window (primary); plus 7-day for faster feedback in burn-rate alerts.

A) Hosted API (multi-tenant)
1) Request success / availability (non-streaming)
- SLI: successful responses / total valid requests
- Success definition (strawman): HTTP 2xx and 4xx that indicate user error (e.g., 400 invalid request) count as “not a platform failure”; 5xx, 408, 429? to be decided; timeouts need classification.
- Target (strawman): 99.90% over 28d for core routes (chat/completions, embeddings)

2) Streaming reliability (chat/completions streaming)
- Candidate SLIs:
  (i) Stream start success: % streams where we send first token / first chunk within threshold
  (ii) Stream completion health: % streams that end cleanly (server closes after final chunk) vs disconnect
- Target (strawman): 99.50% “stream start success”; 99.70% “clean termination” (numbers purely placeholders)

3) Latency
- Non-streaming: p95/p99 end-to-end latency by route (chat/completions; embeddings)
- Streaming: TTFT p95/p99 (primary), plus “token cadence”/stall metrics as secondary.
- Target (strawman): do not set a single latency number across all models; propose percentile targets per “performance class” (small/medium/large) or per-model groups to avoid impossible constraints.

B) Dedicated (reserved capacity, isolated pool)
1) Request success / availability
- Target (strawman): 99.95% over 28d for core routes (chat/completions, embeddings) within a customer’s dedicated pool.
- Stronger stance that 429 due to Redwood protective throttling should be rare; but still may be used as mitigation.

2) Pool readiness / capacity readiness (Dedicated-only)
- SLI: % time pool is “ready to serve” (scheduler healthy + minimum warm capacity + routing path healthy)
- Target (strawman): 99.9% readiness (note: to be validated vs real-world autoscaling/cold-start behavior)
- Need to define what counts as “not ready” (planned maintenance? scale-up in progress? customer-initiated pauses?)

3) Latency
- Similar TTFT vs end-to-end split. But Dedicated should have tighter expectations given isolation; must be realistic given model size and customer-chosen settings.

Important note from Lauren (Dedicated PM): Dedicated customers often care more about p99 stability and “no brownouts” than absolute p95. If we can’t meet strict availability, we need to offer clear mitigations and comms triggers.

Streaming disconnects: initial taxonomy (open)
Goal: stop arguing after incidents about whether “disconnects count.” We need a taxonomy and consistent logging at gateway/runtime.
- Client abort: client closes connection intentionally (navigation, timeout on client, user cancellation).
- Network intermediates: load balancer idle timeout, mobile carrier drops, etc.
- Server-side disconnect: gateway/routing/runtime terminates stream due to error, overload protection, upstream cancellation, or crash.
Open question: do we count client abort as “success” if we already delivered some tokens? Or do we only exclude clear client-cancel signals (explicit cancel endpoint / close with client-sent cancel reason)?

Per-model variance + dimensions (open)
We want dashboards that answer:
- Is this issue only “us-east + model X + streaming” or global?
But we cannot blow up metric cardinality.
Strawman approach:
- Always label tier + route + region.
- Model label: allow in sampled/aggregated form or in a derived dataset for top-N models only.
- For long tail: group into model families or “performance classes.”

Error budgets + enforcement (high-level sketch)
- Compute budget per tier + journey (Hosted chat streaming, Hosted embeddings, Dedicated request success, Dedicated readiness).
- Alert on multi-window burn rates (fast burn vs slow burn).
- Enforcement stages (aligned with Platform):
  1) Warn-only gates in CI and rollouts (pilot services)
  2) Soft-block: require approval/override token when budget is at risk
  3) Hard-block: stop progressive rollout advancement when budget exhausted (except break-glass)
- Mitigation hooks (especially for Hosted):
  - Prefer safe fallbacks when burn spikes (routing)
  - Protective throttling mode to prevent cascading failures (rate limits / admission control)
  - Freeze non-essential feature flags; reduce blast radius

Decisions made in meeting (tentative):
1) We will publish tier principles + strawman SLOs quickly (even if numbers are “initial”) to force alignment, then iterate with backtesting.
2) For streaming latency, TTFT will be the primary SLI (customers notice “nothing happens” first). End-to-end stream duration can be a secondary diagnostic metric.
3) Dedicated must have an explicit readiness SLO (it’s a product promise); but paging behavior will be tuned (ticket vs page) after we see noise.
4) We will pilot enforcement on API gateway + routing/control plane first (because they sit on the critical path and are common sources of widespread incidents).

Open questions (owners + next steps)
1) What is “success” for streaming?
- Question: do partial streams count as success? do we require a minimum token count? how do we handle tool/function calling streams?
- Owner: Aisha Bello + Amara Diallo
- Next: draft disconnect taxonomy + mapping to SLI failure classes; propose “excluded vs counted” list.

2) How to classify 429s, timeouts, and cancellations?
- Question: 429 from quota vs protective throttling vs customer concurrency cap. Which count against availability SLI?
- Owner: Nadia Rahman + Cole Summers
- Next: propose error-class mapping table (HTTP/gRPC) and where classification lives (gateway vs control plane).

3) Latency targets across model sizes
- Question: can we have a single tier latency target if models differ 10x? likely need per-model/per-class.
- Owner: Nikhil Sharma (Hosted PM partner) + Logan Wright
- Next: pull historical TTFT + non-streaming latency distributions by route/model/region; propose target-setting method.

4) Dedicated readiness definition
- Question: define “ready” in a way that reflects customer experience and avoids paging on benign autoscaling transitions.
- Owner: Vanessa Ortiz + Gabe Wilson + Lauren Bishop
- Next: propose readiness SLI components (scheduler health, warm capacity, routing health); identify what’s excluded (planned maintenance windows).

5) Metric dimensions / cardinality budget
- Question: what labels are mandatory vs optional? how do we keep cost sane?
- Owner: Thomas Baird
- Next: labeling proposal + top-N model strategy; recommended aggregation rules.

6) Where do we compute budgets and expose status?
- Question: compute in metrics backend (queries) vs a small budget service/job that writes snapshots; need to support CI checks + console.
- Owner: Ethan Park + Benji Okafor + Jordan Lee
- Next: draft minimal API contract for “budget status by tier/service/journey” that gating can call; propose storage approach.

7) What changes when budget is at risk/exhausted?
- Question: exact thresholds, escalation path, and which change types get frozen.
- Owner: Sean Gallagher + Connor O’Brien + Miles Thornton
- Next: write policy draft with burn-rate thresholds and enforcement actions by tier; include exception/break-glass workflow.

8) Customer comms triggers
- Question: when does budget burn trigger status-page comms vs support-only updates? Dedicated vs Hosted messaging?
- Owner: Marissa Cole + Dev Patel + Rachel Kim
- Next: comms guideline draft; identify what data we can safely expose for Dedicated.

Action items (next 2 weeks)
- Rafael: create Confluence skeleton pages for SLO tables + policy + SLI spec; link this doc.
- Aisha/Amara: first pass streaming disconnect taxonomy + instrumentation gaps.
- Sergio: propose initial dashboard structure (folder naming, required panels, filters for tier/region/route/model where safe).
- Lauren: Dedicated target feedback: what’s realistic short-term; what requires roadmap.
- Jordan/Ethan/Benji: budget-check API sketch + gating flow (warn-only) to unblock pilot planning.

Risks called out
- If we pick targets without backtesting, we risk immediately “living in freeze mode.” Need baseline data and iterative tightening.
- If we over-instrument per-model/per-route, we risk cardinality blowups and unusable queries.
- If enforcement is too strict too early, teams will route around it (or ignore warnings). Need gradual rollout and strong override auditing.

Parking lot (topics we did not resolve)
- How to handle regional capacity constraints that manifest as latency, not errors (and how that should burn budget).
- Whether to define separate SLOs for “model catalog operations” (listing models, fetching model metadata) as part of customer journey.
- Whether Dedicated should have separate SLOs for “provision-to-ready” when customers request pool changes.

Appendix: strawman SLO table template (for Confluence)
For each tier + journey:
- SLO name
- SLI definition (numerator/denominator)
- Target (% or ms)
- Window (28d rolling)
- Dimensions (tier, route, region, model/class)
- Exclusions
- Alerting (burn-rate thresholds)
- Runbook link
- Owner/team

(End of notes; updated 2026-01-28 after follow-up comments from Platform + Dedicated PMs.)
